analysis.one_liner: Requires electric utilities to get 15% of electricity from renewable sources by 2021.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 34 Senate cosponsors and placed on the Senate calendar, never received a vote before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend a 1978 utility law to require electric utilities to draw a rising share of the electricity they sell from renewable sources or energy savings — 3% in 2012, rising to 15% by 2021. Utilities could comply by generating renewable power, buying tradeable credits, using energy-efficiency credits for up to a quarter of their obligation, or paying an alternative compliance fee of 2.1 cents per kilowatt-hour, most of which would go to state renewable energy funds. Small utilities (under 4 million megawatt-hours sold) and Hawaii would be exempt, utilities could get a waiver if compliance costs would raise a customer's bill more than 4%, and the Energy Department could make low-interest loans to help utilities build renewable projects. Introduced in September 2010 with bipartisan cosponsors, it was placed on the Senate calendar but the Senate never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Electricity customers in states with strong renewable resources and wind, solar, geothermal, biomass, hydropower, and waste-to-energy developers, who would gain a guaranteed, growing national market for their output through 2039. The bill's stated purposes include minimizing the impact of the standard on electricity rates for consumers, and it gives utilities ratepayer protections (a waiver if costs would raise bills more than 4% in a year, exemption for small utilities) and access to federal loans to finance compliance projects.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a federal requirement that utilities obtain a rising share of retail electricity from renewable sources or energy efficiency — 3% in 2012–2013, 6% in 2014–2016, 9% in 2017–2018, 12% in 2019–2020, and 15% in 2021–2039 — creating decades of guaranteed demand for renewable generation.

Creates a national tradeable credit market for renewable energy and energy efficiency, letting utilities that over-comply sell credits to those that cannot, which lowers the overall cost of hitting the target.

Includes explicit ratepayer protections: utilities can petition for a waiver if the incremental cost of compliance would exceed 4% per retail customer in a year, small utilities selling under 4 million megawatt-hours are exempt, and 75% of alternative compliance payments flow back to state funds that can offset consumer costs through direct grants or efficiency investments.

Authorizes the Energy Department to make long-term (up to 30-year), low-interest loans to utilities to build renewable facilities and install efficiency technology, with the stated purpose of minimizing the impact on electricity rates for consumers.
Triple credits for small (1 megawatt or less) distributed generators and double credits for generation on Indian land direct compliance value toward community-scale and tribal projects.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil-fuel-fired utilities and their customers in regions with fewer renewable resources, who would face compliance costs — buying credits, building renewable capacity, or paying the 2.1 cents per kilowatt-hour alternative payment — that could be passed through to electricity rates. Existing fossil and nuclear generators would also face a shrinking share of the national electricity market, since the standard excludes most existing hydro, nuclear, and fossil generation from the base quantity utilities must cover with renewables.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would likely be passed through to electricity customers, particularly in regions with limited renewable resources; the bill itself contemplates 'economically harmful increase[s] in electricity rates' by requiring the Energy Secretary to review whether the program caused them.

The compliance structure is generous to incumbents: utilities can meet up to a quarter of the obligation with energy-efficiency credits, can make alternative compliance payments in lieu of actual renewable generation, and can obtain waivers or variances for cost or transmission reasons — so the standard could be satisfied with far less new renewable generation than the headline percentages imply.

The definition of 'renewable energy' includes waste-to-energy combustion, coal-mined methane, and incremental hydropower, which critics argue lets some conventional or polluting sources count toward the target and dilutes the push toward wind and solar.

Biomass provisions open substantial federal and non-federal forest material to harvesting for energy, subject only to sustainability study requirements rather than binding limits — an environmental trade-off some forest advocates would contest.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a real, enforceable national renewable target — one of the stronger designs of its era, with penalties set at 200% of the compliance payment — with numerous pressure valves (efficiency credits, alternative compliance payments, cost waivers, small-utility exemptions) that would blunt its reach, and a flexible 'renewable' definition that includes some non-wind, non-solar sources. The cost would fall on utilities and ratepayers, concentrated in renewable-poor regions, though the 4% rate-impact waiver and federal loan program are explicit attempts to cap consumer pain. On balance it is a genuine push to shift the electricity mix toward renewables with significant escape hatches, rather than a loophole-ridden shell, but how much new renewable capacity it would actually drive depends on how tightly the Energy Department wrote the rules.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in September 2010 with 34 cosponsors and placed on the Senate calendar, the bill sat there until the 111th Congress ended in January 2011 without the Senate ever voting on it.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Bingaman (D-NM), chairman of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, introduced the bill on September 21, 2010, with a list of 34 cosponsors including Republicans Sam Brownback, Susan Collins, John Ensign, and Chuck Grassley.
The bill was read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 576) on September 22, 2010 — the last action ever taken on it.

No committee reported the bill, no floor debate or vote occurred, and the 111th Congress ended January 3, 2011, killing the bill; any version would have had to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil-fuel-fired utilities and the regions that depend on them are better off, because no federal renewable mandate was ever imposed; renewable developers lost a guaranteed national market for at least the next three decades.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil-fuel utilities; no mandate was imposed

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making the bill's 34 cosponsors a majority of the Senate.

against.what_they_did: Opposed federal renewable electricity mandates in the 2010 lame-duck period; the bill never advanced past the calendar to a floor vote.

against.name: Sen. Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but never brought it to the floor for a vote during the 2010 lame-duck session, which was consumed by other priorities.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a bipartisan 34-sponsor list — 29 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 4 Republicans — but with Republicans holding 40 seats and needing only 41 to block a floor vote, no vote was ever scheduled; the sponsor list shows broad agreement, while the absence of floor action in a lame-duck session reflects the partisan line on energy mandates.

industries.industry: Fossil-fuel electric utilities and coal-reliant regions
industries.note: The standard shrinks the market share coal and gas generation can hold and forces their utilities to buy credits, pay compliance fees, or build renewables — costs likely passed to ratepayers. Their regional interest ran against the bill's goal of shifting the grid to renewables.

industries.industry: Wind, solar, geothermal, and marine energy developers
industries.note: A 15% federal standard through 2039 creates guaranteed national demand for their output plus tradeable credits they can sell. The bill's success would have directly expanded their market.

industries.industry: Biomass, waste-to-energy, and landfill gas industries
industries.note: Counted as eligible renewable energy under the bill, with generous credit multipliers for high-efficiency biomass facilities, locking in their role in the compliance market. Some of these sources carry real air-quality and forest-harvesting trade-offs.

Existing hydro is excluded from the base quantity, and incremental hydropower plus new capacity at existing dams counts as qualified renewable, letting hydro operators earn credits without displacing their existing generation.

The bill puts a federal obligation on utilities but also gives them the compliance credit markets, federal low-interest loans, cost waivers, and small-utility exemptions — utilities remain the regulated middlemen through which the national renewable transition would flow.
Existing nuclear is excluded from the base quantity so the standard does not penalize nuclear-heavy utilities, but new nuclear does not count as renewable; the bill neither helps nor hurts them much.
